dmm-2020-individual-01.title: Find the stopping time
dmm-2020-individual-01.body:
Two witches with speeds $u>v$ are at the same spot at time $t$ exactly when $(u-v)t$ is a multiple of $10$. They are together at $t=0$ (first meeting), and the second meeting is at $t=\frac{10}{u-v}$.

The pairs with speed difference $1$ are $(1,2),(2,3),(3,4)$, giving $t=10$; the other pairs have larger differences and meet earlier ($t=5$ or $t=\tfrac{10}{3}$). So every pair has met twice exactly at $t=10$ s.

The total distance is $10\cdot(1+2+3+4)=100$ m.

**Answer: 100**

dmm-2020-individual-01.title: Check the other pairs
dmm-2020-individual-01.body:
The slowest pair to meet twice is the one with the smallest relative speed, $1$ m/s. Since $10/1=10$ s is the largest of all the second-meeting times $10/(u-v)$, the witches stop at $t=10$ s. Each witch travels $10\times$ her speed, total $10(1+2+3+4)=100$.

**Answer: 100**

dmm-2020-individual-02.title: Compare side lengths
dmm-2020-individual-02.body:
Let $A$ have side $a$. The inradius of an equilateral triangle is $r=\dfrac{a}{2\sqrt3}$. An equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle of radius $r$ has side $b=\sqrt3\,r=\dfrac a2$.

Areas of similar figures scale with the square of the side, so $\dfrac{[A]}{[B]}=\left(\dfrac ab\right)^2=2^2=4$.

**Answer: 4**

dmm-2020-individual-02.title: Use the medial triangle
dmm-2020-individual-02.body:
The inscribed circle of $A$ touches the sides at their midpoints, so the midpoints form an equilateral triangle inscribed in $O$ whose side is half of $A$'s side (midline theorem). All equilateral triangles inscribed in $O$ are congruent, so $B$ is this medial triangle. The medial triangle splits $A$ into $4$ congruent triangles, so $[A]/[B]=4$.

**Answer: 4**

dmm-2020-individual-03.title: Chinese remainder theorem
dmm-2020-individual-03.body:
Let $x$ be the number of candies: $x\equiv0\pmod2$, $x\equiv1\pmod7$, $x\equiv6\pmod{11}$, $x\equiv3\pmod{13}$.

From $x\equiv6\pmod{11}$ and $x\equiv3\pmod{13}$: numbers $\equiv3\pmod{13}$ are $3,16,29,\dots$; $94=3+7\cdot13=6+8\cdot11$ works, so $x\equiv94\pmod{143}$.

Combine with evenness: $94$ is even, so $x\equiv94\pmod{286}$. Now $x=94+286t\equiv1\pmod7$: $94\equiv3$, $286\equiv6\equiv-1$, so $3-t\equiv1$, $t\equiv2\pmod7$, giving $x\equiv94+572=666\pmod{2002}$.

The only such number below $2020$ is $666$.

**Answer: 666**

dmm-2020-individual-03.title: Check the candidate
dmm-2020-individual-03.body:
Verify directly: $666=7\cdot95+1$, $666=11\cdot60+6$, $666=13\cdot51+3$, and $666$ is even. The four congruences determine $x$ modulo $2\cdot7\cdot11\cdot13=2002$, so the next solution is $2668>2020$ and $666$ is the only one.

**Answer: 666**

dmm-2020-individual-04.title: Make the rule additive
dmm-2020-individual-04.body:
Put $g(n)=\dfrac{f(n)}{n}$. Dividing $f(mn)=nf(m)+mf(n)$ by $mn$ gives
$$g(mn)=g(m)+g(n).$$
So $g$ turns products into sums, and $g(p)=\dfrac1p$ for primes $p$. Hence for $n=\prod p_i^{e_i}$,
$$g(n)=\sum_i \frac{e_i}{p_i}.$$
For $n=2^2 3^3 5^5 7^7$: $g(n)=\frac22+\frac33+\frac55+\frac77=4$.

**Answer: 4**

dmm-2020-individual-04.title: Compute f of a prime power
dmm-2020-individual-04.body:
By induction $f(p^k)=kp^{k-1}$: indeed $f(p^k)=f(p\cdot p^{k-1})=p^{k-1}f(p)+p\,f(p^{k-1})=p^{k-1}+p(k-1)p^{k-2}=kp^{k-1}$. Then $\dfrac{f(p^k)}{p^k}=\dfrac kp$, and the product rule shows the ratio $f(n)/n$ adds over coprime factors, so $\dfrac{f(n)}n=\dfrac22+\dfrac33+\dfrac55+\dfrac77=4$.

**Answer: 4**

dmm-2020-individual-05.title: Parametrize by the value
dmm-2020-individual-05.body:
Let $N=\dfrac{404}{r^2-4}$ be a positive integer. Then $r^2=4+\dfrac{404}{N}=\dfrac{4(N+101)}{N}$. This is the square of a rational number exactly when $N(N+101)$ is a perfect square, say $N(N+101)=k^2$.

Rewrite as $(2N+101)^2-(2k)^2=101^2=10201$, i.e. $(2N+101-2k)(2N+101+2k)=101\cdot101$. Since $101$ is prime the factor pairs are $(1,10201)$ and $(101,101)$. The pair $(101,101)$ gives $k=0$, $N=0$ (rejected). The pair $(1,10201)$ gives $4N+202=10202$, so $N=2500$.

Check: $r=\frac{51}{25}$ gives $r^2-4=\frac{101}{625}$ and $\frac{404\cdot625}{101}=2500$.

**Answer: 2500**

dmm-2020-individual-05.title: Lowest terms
dmm-2020-individual-05.body:
Write $r=\frac ab$ in lowest terms. Then $\dfrac{404}{r^2-4}=\dfrac{404b^2}{(a-2b)(a+2b)}$. Since $\gcd(a\pm2b,\,b)=1$, we need $(a-2b)(a+2b)\mid404=4\cdot101$. Checking the possibilities, the only one with $b\ne0$ and $\gcd(a,b)=1$ is $a-2b=1,\ a+2b=101$, i.e. $a=51,\ b=25$. Then the value is $404\cdot625/101=2500$.

**Answer: 2500**

dmm-2020-individual-06.title: Telescoping
dmm-2020-individual-06.body:
Since $\alpha$ is a root of $x^2-6x-1=0$, we have $\alpha^2=6\alpha+1$. Then
$$1+\frac{5\alpha+1}{\alpha^k+\alpha}=\frac{\alpha^k+6\alpha+1}{\alpha^k+\alpha}=\frac{\alpha^k+\alpha^2}{\alpha^k+\alpha}=\frac{\alpha^{k-1}+\alpha}{\alpha^{k-1}+1}.$$
With $j=k-1$ the product is $\prod_{j=0}^{\infty}\dfrac{\alpha^j+\alpha}{\alpha^j+1}$. Now $\alpha^j+\alpha=\alpha(\alpha^{j-1}+1)$, so for $j\ge1$ the factor is $\dfrac{\alpha(\alpha^{j-1}+1)}{\alpha^j+1}$ and the product over $j=1,\dots,n$ telescopes to $\dfrac{\alpha^n\cdot 2}{\alpha^n+1}$. Including the $j=0$ factor $\frac{1+\alpha}{2}$:
$$\prod_{j=0}^{n}=\frac{(1+\alpha)\alpha^n}{\alpha^n+1}\longrightarrow 1+\alpha=4+\sqrt{10}.$$
So $m=4$, $n=10$, and $10m+n=50$.

**Answer: 50**

dmm-2020-individual-06.title: Numerical check
dmm-2020-individual-06.body:
The partial products converge extremely fast (the $k$-th factor is $1+O(\alpha^{-k})$ ). Multiplying the first $200$ factors numerically gives $7.16227766\ldots=4+\sqrt{10}$, confirming $m=4$, $n=10$ and $10m+n=50$.

**Answer: 50**

dmm-2020-individual-07.title: Count walks on the triangular lattice
dmm-2020-individual-07.body:
Every interior lattice point has $6$ neighbours, and in $4$ minutes the spider can reach the edge (distance $4$) only by four steps away from the center, so it never touches the boundary earlier. Hence all relevant walks use only interior points with $6$ choices each; there are $6^4=1296$ equally likely walks.

**Reaching the edge.** The number of shortest paths to a boundary point at distance $4$ is $1$ for each of the $6$ corners and $\binom41,\binom42,\binom43=4,6,4$ for the other points on each side: $6+6(4+6+4)=90$.

**Returning to the center.** Let $w(p)$ be the number of $2$-step walks from the center to $p$: $6$ (back to the center), $2$ for each of the $6$ neighbours, $1$ for each of the $6$ corner points at distance $2$, and $2$ for each of the $6$ mid-side points at distance $2$ (total $36$). The number of closed $4$-step walks is $\sum_p w(p)^2=36+6\cdot4+6\cdot1+6\cdot4=90$.

So the probability is $\dfrac{90+90}{1296}=\dfrac{5}{36}$ and $m+n=41$.

**Answer: 41**

dmm-2020-individual-07.title: Direct computation
dmm-2020-individual-07.body:
Track the distribution of the spider's position for four steps exactly (a short computer enumeration of the walk on the triangular lattice) gives probability $\frac{5}{36}$ of being at the center or on the edge after $4$ steps, confirming $m+n=5+36=41$.

**Answer: 41**

dmm-2020-individual-08.title: Power of a point and Stewart
dmm-2020-individual-08.body:
Let $x=BC$. By power of a point, $BF\cdot FD=AF\cdot FC=2\cdot10=20$ and $BG\cdot GE=AG\cdot GC=8\cdot4=32$.

Since $DE\parallel FG$, triangles $BFG$ and $BDE$ are similar, so $\dfrac{BF}{FD}=\dfrac{BG}{GE}$. Multiply both sides' numerator and denominator by $BF$ and $BG$ respectively: $\dfrac{BF^2}{BF\cdot FD}=\dfrac{BG^2}{BG\cdot GE}$, i.e. $\dfrac{BF^2}{20}=\dfrac{BG^2}{32}$.

Stewart's theorem on cevians of side $AC=12$:
$$BF^2=\frac{AB^2\cdot FC+BC^2\cdot AF}{AC}-AF\cdot FC=\frac{1000+2x^2}{12}-20=\frac{760+2x^2}{12},$$
$$BG^2=\frac{AB^2\cdot GC+BC^2\cdot AG}{AC}-AG\cdot GC=\frac{400+8x^2}{12}-32=\frac{16+8x^2}{12}.$$
Then $\dfrac{760+2x^2}{20}=\dfrac{16+8x^2}{32}$, so $8(760+2x^2)=5(16+8x^2)$, i.e. $6000=24x^2$ and $x^2=250$.

**Answer: 250**

dmm-2020-individual-08.title: Similar triangles
dmm-2020-individual-08.body:
Let $x=BC$, $p=BF$, $q=DF$, $u=BG$, $v=GE$, $y=CD=AE$ (the trapezoid $ACED$ is isosceles). From $\triangle ABF\sim\triangle DCF$: $\frac{q}{2}=\frac{y}{10}=\frac{10}{p}$, so $q=\frac y5$, $p=\frac{100}{y}$. From $\triangle BCG\sim\triangle AEG$: $\frac yx=\frac v4=\frac8u$, so $v=\frac{4y}x$, $u=\frac{8x}{y}$. Parallelism gives $\frac pq=\frac uv$: $\frac{500}{y^2}=\frac{2x^2}{y^2}$, so $x^2=250$.

**Answer: 250**

dmm-2020-individual-09.title: Casework on group sizes
dmm-2020-individual-09.body:
The $6$ people split into $3$ non-empty groups in $S(6,3)=90$ equally likely ways, by size type $(4,1,1)$: $15$ ways, $(3,2,1)$: $60$ ways, $(2,2,2)$: $15$ ways.

A group qualifies when it has at least one angel and no more angels than devils.

* $(4,1,1)$: singletons never qualify, so the group of $4$ must contain both devils and $2$ angels, so the two singletons are angels: $\binom42=6$ ways.
* $(3,2,1)$: the triple qualifies only if it holds both devils (and one angel); the pair qualifies only if it is one devil and one angel (a pair of devils has no angel); the singleton never qualifies. Both devils in the triple: choose its angel ($4$ ways) and the pair from the other $3$ angels ($3$ ways), $12$ ways. Pair = one devil and one angel: $2\cdot4=8$ ways, and the remaining $4$ people split into triple and singleton in $4$ ways, $32$ ways. The two cases cannot overlap, so $44$ qualify.
* $(2,2,2)$: if the devils are together, the other two pairs are angel pairs (not qualifying) and the devil pair has no angel, so fails; otherwise each devil is with an angel: $15-3=12$ qualifying.

Total $6+44+12=62$ of $90$, so $p=\frac{62}{90}=\frac{31}{45}$ and $m+n=76$.

**Answer: 76**

dmm-2020-individual-09.title: Complement
dmm-2020-individual-09.body:
Count the bad splits instead: $(4,1,1)$: $15-6=9$; $(3,2,1)$: $60-44=16$; $(2,2,2)$: $3$ (the two devils together). That is $28$ bad splits, so the good ones number $90-28=62$ (a computer enumeration of all $90$ partitions agrees), $p=\frac{62}{90}=\frac{31}{45}$ and $m+n=76$.

**Answer: 76**

dmm-2020-individual-10.title: Leading digits of powers of 2
dmm-2020-individual-10.body:
If $N$ has leading digit $c$ and $k$ digits, then $c\cdot10^{k-1}\le N<(c+1)10^{k-1}$, so $2N$ has leading digit between that of $2c$ and that of $2c+1$. Applying this to powers of two starting from a power with leading digit $1$, the leading digits until the next power with leading digit $1$ follow one of the patterns $1,2,4,8,1$; $1,2,4,9,1$; $1,2,5,1$; $1,3,6,1$; $1,3,7,1$.

So each digit length contains exactly one power of $2$ beginning with $1$, and consecutive such powers differ in exponent by $3$ (patterns $3$-$5$, no leading $4$) or by $4$ (patterns $1$-$2$, exactly one leading $4$).

$2^0$ (1 digit) and $2^{21998}=2^{22000}/4$ (leading digits $1.14\ldots$, with $6623$ digits) both begin with $1$, so there are $6622$ steps with total exponent increase $21998$. If $t$ steps have length $4$, then $3\cdot6622+t=21998$, so $t=2132$. Each length-$4$ step contains exactly one power starting with $4$, and $2^{21999}$ starts with $2$, so the range $1\le n<22000$ contains exactly $2132$ such powers.

**Answer: 2132**

dmm-2020-individual-10.title: Exact computation
dmm-2020-individual-10.body:
Computing $2^n$ exactly for $n=1,\dots,21999$ and counting those whose decimal expansion begins with $4$ gives $2132$ (the pattern argument explains why: one such $n$ for each exponent gap of $4$ between consecutive powers beginning with $1$).

**Answer: 2132**
